[MUQATIL:41:36-38/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Created signs make God's oneness knowable through His workmanship even though He is unseen.
[MUQATIL:41:36-38/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The sun and moon are created signs, so worship belongs to their creator rather than to them.
[MUQATIL:41:36-38/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The Prophet and believers prostrated, prompting Meccan polytheists to say they would instead worship al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat.
[MAJAZ:v2p197/r1] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The feminine plural pronoun refers to night, day, sun, and moon; after mentioning the sun and moon as objects of worship, the verse redirects worship to their Creator. Mixed or collective groups are expressed in the feminine.
[TAB-FULL:v20p436/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The alternation of night and day and the sun and moon are signs proving God’s oneness and immense sovereignty; the sun does not overtake the moon, and each moves in its orbit. | mentions 36:40
[TAB-FULL:v20p436/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The luminaries move only by God’s direction and cannot independently benefit or harm; worship belongs to God, who could remove their light and leave people lost in darkness.
[TAB-FULL:v20p436/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The feminine plural pronoun refers to the four things named—night, day, sun, and moon; Arabic commonly uses feminine agreement for nonhuman plurals.
[TAB-FULL:v20p437/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Worshipping God means humbling oneself in obedience and dedicating worship to Him alone, without associating anything with Him. | mentions 2:172
[ZAJJAJ:v4p387/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The night, day, sun, and moon are signs that show God is one.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p387/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The feminine pronoun may refer to non-rational plurals, which take feminine agreement; a masculine plural pronoun is reserved for rational beings.
[ZAJJAJ:v4p387/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Alternatively, the feminine pronoun refers to the implied feminine plural āyāt, since the listed objects are called God's signs.
[SULAMI:v2p220/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says signs are shown so people seek their Manifestor; attending to the signs distracts from Him, while attending to Him prevents other distractions.
[THALABI:v8p297/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The feminine plural pronoun in خلقهن follows a broken plural for non-rational things rather than masculine-over-feminine agreement.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p183/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Night and day are signs through their stable measure and ordered alternation, serving wisdom and benefit.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p183/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The sun and moon are signs through distinctive light and the governance and measure displayed in them.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p183/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says “them” refers to the signs just mentioned.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p183/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن مسعود والحسن | reports | Ibn Masud and al-Hasan place the prostration at the end of “if you worship Him.”
[QUSHAYRI:v3p152/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The alternation of night and day and the courses of sun and moon are signs of God’s power and proofs of His oneness.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p152/r2] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The sun’s height and the moon’s brightness are no grounds for worship; God is jealous for the servant’s devotion and commands prostration to their Creator.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p152/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Although sun and moon are lofty and beautiful, they were created for human benefit, so people should worship their Creator rather than them.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p152/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | God commanded the angels, despite their abundant worship and precedence in obedience, to bow to Adam; by contrast, He tells sinful human descendants not to bow to sun and moon.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p152/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The command to protect one’s face from sun and moon exposes the indignity of moving one’s feet for every base desire and presenting oneself before everyone.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p271/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | A singular “moon” is not genuinely indefinite, since there is only one moon; “crescent” can be indefinite more fully because multiple crescents exist.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p271/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The Qur’an uses the plural for crescents but not moon, illustrating the difference between the forms. | mentions 2:189
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p271/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Al-Buhturi provides what Jurjani calls a subtle example of indefinite wording with his phrase “two moons.”
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p271/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Jurjani finds Abu Tammam’s moon image awkward because it suggests multiple moons that are both far away and near in brightness.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p271/r5] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The sense works better with a definite moon, as in al-Buhturi’s line: despite its great height, its light is close to night travelers.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p271/r6] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | One can force a new sentence after “a moon,” but the phrasing still sits badly with the intended meaning.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p271/r7] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · سعيد بن حميد | reports | Saʿid b. Humayd’s poem says he arranged a visit at night because that is the customary time for the moon to rise.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p271/r8] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | reports | Asked why he prefers night over bright day, the speaker answers that he does not want to change the established custom of moonrise.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p271/r9] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | reports | Jurjani gives an opposing dawn version: the beloved comes in the morning because she is the sun, which rises then.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p175#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Night, day, sun, and moon are signs of God's power; worship God alone rather than prostrating to the sun or moon.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p175#2/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The feminine plural pronoun khalaqahunna follows the broken-plural construction and does not use masculine predominance over feminine nouns.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p16#3/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · فرقة | reports | A third group refers the pronoun to all four objects; non-rational plurals below ten may take this feminine plural agreement.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p16#3/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The example from 9:36 shows feminine plural agreement with a non-rational plural. | mentions 9:36
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p16#3/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Ibn Atiyya cites Hassan ibn Thabit’s line as another grammatical example of feminine plural agreement; its words continue in the next segment.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p16#3/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Night and day invite reflection on changing lengths, overlap, and equality in different places; sun and moon display wonders, divine wisdom, and benefit to people.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p16#3/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Even useful celestial bodies should not be worshipped: their benefit comes from God’s subjection of them, so God alone deserves prostration.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p16#3/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · فرقة | reports | One group says the plural pronoun refers to the days mentioned earlier.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p16#3/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · فرقة | reports | Another group takes the pronoun to refer to the sun and moon, treating a pair as a plural and non-rational plurals as feminine.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p16#3/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Because Arabic uses the plurals shumūs and aqmār for the celestial bodies, the collective plural agreement is possible for sun and moon.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Night is the sun's departure from the earth's surface, and day its rising over it; both follow stable measures and an enduring order.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The sun and moon have distinctive lights and display ordered motion in their courses.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Despite their many benefits, the sun and moon are not creators and must not be worshipped.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The feminine plural pronoun can refer to a nonrational plural, which may take feminine singular or plural agreement, as in his example about sheep.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Alternatively, the pronoun refers to the meaning of آيات, since the verse introduces these objects as God's signs.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | If they truly intend to worship God, they must prostrate to Him alone and no other.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r19] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن مسعود والحسن | reports | Ibn Masʿūd and al-Ḥasan place the prostration-of-recitation after إن كنتم إياه تعبدون; Abū ʿAmr chooses this placement, also reported from the Imams.
[TABRISI:41:36-39/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | These are proofs of God's oneness and signs of attributes by which He differs from all creatures.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p111/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The preceding verse commends the best deeds and calling to God; this verse follows with signs of God's existence, power, and wisdom, since calling to Him entails presenting proofs of His essence and attributes.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p111/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Night is mentioned before day because darkness is nonexistence and light is existence, and nonexistence precedes existence, hinting that these phenomena began to exist.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p111/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Celestial bodies and other created parts of the world prove the Creator; Al-Razi points to his earlier explanations in al-Fatiha and al-Anam. | mentions 1:2, 6:1

I-FULL:v27p111/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The sun and moon are created servants and signs of the powerful God, so prostration, the highest reverence, belongs only to the Creator.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p111/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Some people, including star-worshipping Sabians, claimed prostrating to the sun and moon was a means of prostrating to God; the verse forbids that intermediary and directs worship only to the Maker.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p111/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Razi assigns the feminine plural pronoun to night, day, and moon; nonrational plural nouns take feminine agreement, and من آياته is also treated as feminine.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p111/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although one might propose the sun as a prayer direction, habitual prostration toward its exalted, luminous body could make people think the sun is worshipped.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p111/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A stone can serve as a qibla without suggesting divinity, so the intended benefit of orientation remains while the risk associated with the sun disappears.
[RAZI-FULL:v27p111/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafii locates the prostration verse at تعبدون because واسجدوا لله connects to it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Night, day, sun, and moon are signs pointing to God's oneness and power.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | There is consensus that the passage is a prostration verse, though authorities disagree about exactly where to prostrate.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Malik places the prostration at 'if you worship Him,' because it is connected to the command; Ali, Ibn Masʿud, and others did likewise.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r16] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن العربي | holds | Ibn al-Arabi says the disagreement about the prostration point is a minor matter.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r17] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن خويزمنداد | reports | Ibn Khuwayz Mandad says the verse includes lunar and solar eclipse prayer because Arabs associated eclipses with the death of a great person, prompting the Prophet's prayer.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r18] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Qurtubi confirms eclipse prayer in al-Bukhari and Muslim; its forms vary with reports, and Sahih Muslim is the authority on the subject.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The celestial bodies do not deserve worship by their own virtue; God created them and could erase or extinguish them.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The pronoun in khalaqahunna returns to sun, moon, night, and day.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | An alternative takes the pronoun as referring only to the sun and moon, with a dual referred to in plural form.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Another alternative makes the pronoun refer to the meaning of āyāt, signs.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The feminine plural follows a plural of non-rational beings rather than applying masculine-feminine prevalence.
[QURTUBI-FULL:41:37-39/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | If they worship God, they should prostrate to Him alone, the one who created, formed, and subjected these signs.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:41:36-37/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Night, day, sun, and moon are signs of God.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:41:36-37/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | They are creatures subject to command, just as humans are, so they are not to be worshipped.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:41:36-37/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The pronoun refers to all four preceding signs; mentioning them together suggests that they belong among things without knowledge or choice.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:41:36-37/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Worship God who created them; prostration is the most specific form of worship.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:41:36-37/r9] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The author places the prostration of recitation at this verse because it contains the command; Abu Hanifa places it at the end of the following verse, where the meaning is complete.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p91#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Night and day point to oneness through their measured succession and alternation; sun and moon do so through their assigned courses and fixed light.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p91#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The sun and moon are created beings, despite their many benefits, so they are not to be worshipped.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p91#2/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The feminine plural pronoun refers either to the signs or to the four non-rational entities; such plurals take feminine agreement, as in the examples about pens.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p91#2/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Some people, like the star-worshipping Sabians, prostrated to sun and moon while claiming to intend Allah; the verse forbids this intermediary and demands worship directed purely to Allah.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p91#2/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | If someone worships another alongside Allah, he is not truly worshipping Allah; the command requires exclusive monotheism.
[QASHANI:41:36-39/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Night is the self's darkness veiling the light and making one prone to sins and satanic whispers; day is the spirit's light shining from the heart, enabling good deeds, resistance to evil, and receptivity to divine breezes.
[QASHANI:41:36-39/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The sun is the spirit; one must not annihilate in it and stop there, becoming veiled from the Real.
[QASHANI:41:36-39/r6] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The moon is the heart; one must not stop with its virtues and perfections or incline to the Paradise of attributes.
[QASHANI:41:36-39/r7] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | True prostration is annihilation in the divine essence, reserving worship for God alone in un veiled unity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p307/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | After presenting calling to God as the best speech and action, the text adduces celestial and terrestrial signs as proof of God's power, wisdom, and case.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p307/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Night comes first because darkness is absence while light is existence; the sun follows the day because it illuminates the world more than the moon, whose light is said to derive from the sun.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p307/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Some people worshipped the sun, as in the account of the Queen of Sheba and her people. | mentions 27:24
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p307/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | He explains the feminine plural pronoun “them” as agreement with an unintelligent plural understood as feminine.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p307/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | He says al-Zamakhshari's explanation should distinguish small plurals from large ones; the passage coordinates four entities rather than a single plural noun.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p307/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | He also says “them” returns to the implied plural āyāt in “among His signs.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p307/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Other explanations return the pronoun to the signs just mentioned, or to sun and moon, which can be treated as a plural because of their differing cycles.
[SAMIN-DURR:41:37/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari lets the feminine plural pronoun refer to all four coordinated objects because nonrational plurals may take feminine agreement; the Sheikh says he fails to distinguish plurals of paucity from abundance.
[SAMIN-DURR:41:37/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | reports | The Sheikh says nonrational plurals of paucity most properly take feminine plural agreement, while plurals of abundance take feminine singular; these four separate coordinated nouns function like one plural expression.
[SAMIN-DURR:41:37/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The author replies that al-Zamakhshari explains why feminine agreement occurs despite three masculine and one feminine antecedents: masculine normally prevails, or the referent is the feminine plural آيات.
[SAMIN-DURR:41:37/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari also allows the pronoun to refer to the implied feminine plural آيات in ومن آياته.
[SAMIN-DURR:41:37/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A third referent is the sun and moon: the dual is treated as a plural, and Arabic has the plurals شموس and أقمار.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p182/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Alternating night and day, the sun, and the moon’s changing course and phases let people measure days, months, and years and know when rights, worship, and transactions are due.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p182/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The sun and moon are among the finest visible bodies, yet are created servants under God’s power; worship belongs to God alone, since associating partners with Him is not forgiven.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p182/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · جابر | reports | Jabir reports that the Prophet forbade cursing night, day, sun, moon, and winds, since they may be sent as mercy to some people and punishment to others.
[BURHAN:v2p131/r10] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Rising stars attract idolaters by their splendor; the sun's setting is retreat, and it rises and sets between Satan's horns, while revelation forbids its worship. | mentions 18:90, 41:37
[BURHAN:v2p131/r11] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Repentance remains open until the sun rises from the East; the people exposed to it are captivated, though worship of sun and moon is forbidden. | mentions 18:90
[BURHAN:v3p233/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Putting إياه before تعبدون preserves the cadence and so

und pattern of the verse endings.
[BURHAN:v3p366/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · قيل | reports | One explanation takes the feminine plural pronoun in خلقهن back to the signs just mentioned: night, day, sun, and moon.
[BURHAN:v3p366/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · البغوي | reports | Al-Baghawi says خلقهن uses feminine agreement with a broken plural of non-rational things rather than masculine-over-feminine agreement.
[BURHAN:v4p93#2/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | When the same definite noun is repeated, the second usually refers to the first; examples include hardship in 94:5–6, the path in the Fatiha, and celestial objects in 41:37.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | True worship must belong exclusively to God: prostrating even once to another makes the worship shirk, and God accepts only sincere worship because He is utterly self-sufficient.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r11] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Their claim that they worship idols only to bring them nearer to God (39:3) conflicts with their own exclusive invocations in distress, especially at sea. | mentions 39:3
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r12] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The verse urges people to preserve human dignity by never prostrating to a creature: angels were commanded to prostrate to Adam, while Iblīs refused, marking opposite stations.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | After describing the polytheists' idols and the virtue of prayer, the author presents cosmic signs as proofs of monotheism that dispel all rivals and illuminate God's essence and attributes through His acts.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Night and day, sun and moon are signs of God's oneness; their arrangement demonstrates power over resurrection and every possible thing.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Night precedes day because darkness is nonexistence and light is existence; the sun and moon are like the spirit of night and day, their bodies.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | reports | An unnamed poetic saying calls the created universe a message from the highest King to humanity and says everything besides God is vain.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The repeated negation stresses that each object is separately forbidden, and the moon is named explicitly instead of being left to a pronoun.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The sun is described as the greatest of the worshippers' idols, though it too is one of God's created things.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Only God, possessor of every perfection without defect, deserves prostration because He created the four signs; the feminine plural pronoun follows the convention for inanimate things and underscores their lowliness as deities.
[BIQAI-FULL:v6p574/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | He entertains another explanation for the feminine plural: the moon is counted as multiple moons because it changes through crescent, full, and dark phases.
[BURSEVI:v8p202#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | ‘Among His signs’ means signs of God’s power.
[BURSEVI:v8p202#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الإمام المرزوقي | reports | Al-Marzūqī pairs night with day and the night with the daytime period.
[BURSEVI:v8p202#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The sun accompanies daytime and the moon nighttime; both are creatures subjected to God’s command.
[BURSEVI:v8p202#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Their alternation and subjection serve creatures’ needs and plainly demonstrate God’s existence, oneness, knowledge, and wisdom.
[BURSEVI:v8p202#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The signs invite the seeker to look now with the heart’s eye at God’s workmanship, including the revival of the earth and the lengthening of the shade, in hope of seeing Him by His grace in the hereafter. | mentions 30:50, 25:45, 75:22
[BURSEVI:v8p202#3/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Do not prostrate to the sun or moon because they are created beings subjected to commands just as humans are.
[BURSEVI:v8p202#3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أهل الظاهر | reports | For outward interpreters, the command is creational rather than a legal command, since the sun and moon lack knowledge and choice.
[BURSEVI:v8p202#3/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أهل الحقيقة | holds | For the people of spiritual reality the matter is otherwise: all creation is obedient, so fairness requires the human seeker to obey as well, as Saʿdī’s verse says.
